stem: The student wants to introduce the Teversham pattern book to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The Teversham pattern book is a bound volume of fabric samples.
- Calico printers in Lancashire, England, assembled it between 1781 and 1786.
- It contains 412 swatches of block-printed cotton.
- It was rediscovered in 1959 in a solicitor's office.
- It was digitized in 2014, and the swatches can now be viewed online.
choices: Rediscovered in a solicitor's office in 1959, the Teversham pattern book was later digitized in 2014 for online viewing.
The Teversham pattern book, a bound volume of fabric samples, was assembled in 1959 by those who rediscovered it.
The Teversham pattern book, a bound volume of 412 block-printed cotton swatches, was assembled by Lancashire calico printers.
Since 2014, the 412 swatches in the Teversham pattern book have been digitized so that anyone can view them online.
explanation: Someone who has never heard of the Teversham pattern book first needs to know what it is. Choice C attaches a category label right after the name (a bound volume of block-printed cotton swatches) and then says who made it. That is the identifying description an unfamiliar reader needs.

A.why: You picked a choice built on secondary dates, the 1959 rediscovery and the 2014 digitization. It never says that the book is a volume of fabric samples, so a new reader still doesn't know what was rediscovered.

B.why: You went for the right label but missed a misattribution. The notes say Lancashire calico printers assembled the book in the 1780s. It was only rediscovered in 1959, and the people who found it didn't assemble it.

D.why: You picked a choice about a later development, the digitization. It treats the book as something the reader already knows and never says what kind of object it is or where it came from.

stem: The student wants to introduce the Callan Panel to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The Callan Panel is a longitudinal survey.
- Since 1998, it has followed the same 9,000 workers in Ireland.
- Participants report their earnings and any job changes every two years.
- In 2019, economist Nuala Breen used Callan Panel data to show that workers who switched employers earned 11 percent more, on average, than workers who stayed.
- A spin-off survey, the Callan Youth Panel, began in 2012.
choices: The Callan Panel, a longitudinal survey, has tracked the earnings and job changes of the same 9,000 Irish workers since 1998.
Using Callan Panel data, economist Nuala Breen found in 2019 that employer-switchers earned 11 percent more than stayers.
The Callan Youth Panel, a spin-off survey, began in 2012, fourteen years after the original Callan Panel was launched.
The Callan Panel, a longitudinal survey of 9,000 workers, has shown that changing employers raises pay for all Irish workers.
explanation: A reader who doesn't know the Callan Panel needs to know what it is and what it does. Choice A gives the category (a longitudinal survey) and explains what it does: it tracks the same 9,000 Irish workers' earnings and job changes over time.

B.why: You picked a single finding drawn from the panel. The sentence assumes the reader already knows what the Callan Panel is and never explains that it's a long-running survey of workers.

C.why: You were caught by the offshoot detail. This sentence is about the Youth Panel and a date. It never says what the original Callan Panel is or what it measures.

D.why: You accepted a claim the notes don't support. One study found an average 11 percent gain for switchers. That doesn't mean switching raises pay for all Irish workers, and the survey itself doesn't 'show' findings.

stem: The student wants to introduce the Prentiss Satiety Score to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The Prentiss Satiety Score is a rating system for foods.
- It ranks foods by how long a fixed 240-calorie serving keeps people from feeling hungry.
- Nutrition scientist Ada Prentiss developed it in 1994.
- Of the 38 foods first tested, boiled potatoes scored highest and croissants scored lowest.
- A 2011 revision added 60 more foods.
choices: Of the 38 foods first rated with the Prentiss Satiety Score, boiled potatoes scored highest and croissants scored lowest.
A 2011 revision of the Prentiss Satiety Score, first developed in 1994, added 60 foods to the original 38.
The Prentiss Satiety Score, developed in 1994, ranks foods by how many calories they contain per 240-gram serving.
Developed by Ada Prentiss in 1994, the Prentiss Satiety Score ranks foods by how long a 240-calorie serving staves off hunger.
explanation: An unfamiliar reader needs to know what the score measures. Choice D names the score and gives its purpose: it ranks foods by how long a fixed 240-calorie serving keeps hunger away. It also says who developed it and when.

A.why: You picked a choice built on results. It reports which foods scored highest and lowest but assumes the reader already knows what the score measures, which this audience doesn't.

B.why: You went for dates and a later revision. The sentence counts how many foods were added but never says what the score actually rates.

C.why: You missed a reversal. The calorie amount is held fixed at 240, and the score measures how long that serving keeps hunger away. It doesn't measure calorie content, and the serving is 240 calories, not 240 grams.

stem: The student wants to introduce Velunaria to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Velunaria is an extinct genus of seed fern.
- Seed ferns were plants with fern-like leaves that reproduced by seeds rather than spores.
- Velunaria fossils date to about 280 million years ago.
- The first specimen was found in 1934 in a Kansas coal seam.
- In 2016, paleobotanist Lena Ortiz reclassified two Velunaria species.
choices: Velunaria, an extinct seed fern, was a plant with fern-like leaves that reproduced by seeds rather than by spores.
First found in a Kansas coal seam in 1934, fossils of Velunaria date to about 280 million years ago.
In 2016, paleobotanist Lena Ortiz reclassified two species belonging to the seed fern genus Velunaria.
Velunaria, an extinct seed fern, was a plant with fern-like leaves that reproduced by spores rather than by seeds.
explanation: There are two steps here. A new reader needs the label (an extinct seed fern), and because 'seed fern' is itself an unfamiliar term, they also need to know what that means. Choice A does both: it names the category and explains that these plants had fern-like leaves but reproduced by seeds.

B.why: You picked a choice made of a discovery date and a fossil age. It never says what kind of organism Velunaria was, so a new reader can't tell whether it was a plant, an animal, or something else.

C.why: You picked a narrow later development. It mentions 'seed fern' but leaves that term unexplained and focuses on a reclassification that only matters to a reader who already knows the genus.

D.why: You missed a reversal in the definition. The notes say seed ferns reproduced by seeds rather than spores, which is exactly what sets them apart. This choice gets it backward.

A facsimile edition of the Ruiz-Pell Atlas, originally produced between 1871 and 1879, was printed in 1998.
The Ruiz-Pell Atlas, a set of 64 hand-drawn maps, shows water depths taken by Ruiz and coastlines drawn by Pell.
The Ruiz-Pell Atlas, a set of 64 hand-drawn maps made in the 1870s, charts tidal channels around Chile's Chiloe archipelago.

B.why: You went for the dates of production and reprinting. A new reader learns that a facsimile exists but not what the atlas is or what it maps.

The Corvo Array, an 18-dish radio telescope in the Azores, detects fast radio bursts, brief radio flashes from distant galaxies.

stem: The student wants to introduce Tessaline to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Tessaline is a technique for weaving cloth from linen and wool fibers twisted together into a single thread.
• It was developed in the 1840s by weavers in the Flemish town of Oudebeke.
• Tessaline cloth was warmer than linen but lighter than wool.
• In 1871, a guild of Tessaline weavers founded the Oudebeke Textile School.
• The school still offers summer courses in the technique.
choices: In 1871, a guild of Tessaline weavers founded the Oudebeke Textile School, which still offers summer courses today.
Tessaline, a technique for weaving cloth from twisted linen and wool fibers, was developed by weavers in Oudebeke in the 1840s.
Tessaline was warmer than linen but lighter than wool, an advantage that its Oudebeke inventors had not expected.
The Oudebeke Textile School, which still offers summer courses, is where Tessaline was first developed in 1871.
explanation: Your goal is to introduce Tessaline to readers who have never heard of it, so they first need to know what it is. Choice B names Tessaline and gives it a label in an appositive, "a technique for weaving cloth from twisted linen and wool fibers." It then adds where and when the technique began. Someone new to the topic finishes the sentence knowing what Tessaline is.

A.why: You went for a later detail, the school the weavers founded, and missed that this choice never says what Tessaline is. It mentions "Tessaline weavers" as if the reader already knows the term, so it doesn't work for an unfamiliar audience.

C.why: You picked a sentence that describes the cloth's qualities but never explains that Tessaline is a weaving technique. It also claims the inventors "had not expected" this advantage, and the notes never say that.

D.why: You mixed up two notes. Weavers in Oudebeke developed Tessaline in the 1840s. The school came later, in 1871, so the technique wasn't first developed there. This choice also never says what Tessaline is.

stem: The student wants to introduce Ashmere Cairn to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

• In 2022, a team surveyed the surrounding fields using ground-penetrating radar.

Ashmere Cairn, a Bronze Age burial monument in western Scotland, is a stone mound built over a chamber for the dead.
Ashmere Cairn, a Bronze Age timber hall in western Scotland, was first excavated by archaeologists in 1911.

B.why: You went for the most striking discovery in the notes. But the timber hall is a nearby find, not the cairn. This sentence describes the cairn's surroundings and never says what the cairn is.

stem: The student wants to introduce Langerhans cells to an audience unfamiliar with them. Which choice does NOT effectively use relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Langerhans cells are immune cells found in the outer layer of the skin.
• They capture foreign particles that enter the skin and carry them to nearby lymph nodes.
• There, they present the particles to T cells, alerting the immune system to a possible threat.
• The cells were first described in 1868 by Paul Langerhans, a German medical student.
• Langerhans initially mistook them for nerve cells because of their branching shape.
choices: Langerhans cells, immune cells in the skin's outer layer, capture foreign particles and carry them to nearby lymph nodes.
Found in the outer layer of the skin, Langerhans cells are immune cells that alert T cells to foreign particles.
Langerhans cells were mistaken for nerve cells by Paul Langerhans, who first described them as a student in 1868.
Langerhans cells are skin-dwelling immune cells that warn the body of threats by presenting captured particles to T cells.
explanation: The goal is to introduce Langerhans cells to readers who have never heard of them, so a choice has to say what they are. Choice C uses only the history notes: who described the cells, when, and what he mistook them for. It never says they are immune cells or what they do. A new reader finishes it knowing only what Langerhans cells are not, so C is the one that fails the goal.

A.why: You may have marked this as failing because it leaves out T cells and the history. But an introduction doesn't need every note. The appositive 'immune cells in the skin's outer layer' tells a new reader what the cells are, and the rest of the sentence says what they do. That accomplishes the goal.

B.why: You may have thought 'alert T cells' goes beyond the notes. It doesn't: the notes say the cells present particles to T cells and alert the immune system. The opening modifier and 'are immune cells' give the label a new reader needs, so this choice works.

D.why: You may have read 'skin-dwelling' or 'warn the body of threats' as a change to the notes. Both are accurate paraphrases of 'found in the outer layer of the skin' and 'alerting the immune system to a possible threat.' The sentence names the cells and labels them as immune cells, so it accomplishes the goal.

stem: The student wants to introduce the Marrow Street Collection to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Marrow Street Collection is an archive of field recordings of work songs sung by dockworkers.
• Musicologist Teodora Lind assembled it between 1958 and 1971.
• It holds 1,140 recordings; the next-largest archive of dockworkers' songs holds about 400.
• In 2019, a university library digitized 600 of the recordings.
• A spin-off project, Harbor Voices, trains choirs to perform the songs.
choices: With 1,140 recordings, the Marrow Street Collection holds nearly three times as many as the next-largest archive of its kind.
The Marrow Street Collection, an archive of field recordings of dockworkers' work songs, was assembled by musicologist Teodora Lind.
After a university library digitized 600 of its recordings in 2019, the Marrow Street Collection inspired the choir project Harbor Voices.
Musicologist Teodora Lind spent thirteen years assembling the Marrow Street Collection, the largest archive of field recordings in the world.
explanation: A reader who has never heard of the Marrow Street Collection first needs to know what it is. Choice B names it and adds an appositive label right away: it's an archive of field recordings of dockworkers' work songs. It also says who assembled it. That's the identifying description the goal asks for.

A.why: You went for the comparison between the two archive sizes. It's a striking gap, but the choice never says what the collection holds, so a new reader still doesn't know what it is.

C.why: You picked secondary details, the digitization and the spin-off project. The choice treats the collection as something the reader already knows and never says what it is.

D.why: The notes say only that it's larger than the next-largest archive of dockworkers' songs, not that it's the largest archive of field recordings in the world. This choice claims more than the notes support.

stem: The student wants to introduce haboobs to an audience unfamiliar with them. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A haboob is an intense dust storm driven by the cold outflow of a collapsing thunderstorm.
• Its leading edge can form a wall of dust more than 1,000 meters high.
• The name comes from an Arabic word meaning "blowing."
• Haboobs are common in Sudan and the southwestern United States.
• One regional study counted about 24 haboobs a year in central Sudan and about 3 a year near Phoenix, Arizona.
choices: Haboobs, whose name comes from an Arabic word meaning "blowing," are far more frequent in central Sudan than near Phoenix.
Central Sudan sees about 24 haboobs a year, roughly eight times as many as the area near Phoenix, Arizona.
A haboob, an intense dust storm driven by the cold outflow of a collapsing thunderstorm, can raise a wall of dust over 1,000 meters high.
Because haboobs form only in Sudan and the southwestern United States, most people elsewhere have never seen one.
explanation: A new reader needs to know what a haboob is before anything else. Choice C attaches the category label right after the name in an appositive: an intense dust storm driven by a collapsing thunderstorm's cold outflow. It then adds one vivid detail. It's the only choice that tells an unfamiliar reader what the term means.

A.why: You were drawn to the name's origin and the frequency contrast. The choice explains the word but never the thing, so it assumes the reader already knows a haboob is a dust storm.

B.why: You answered about the gap between the two regions' counts. The math holds up, but the choice never says what a haboob is, which is what this audience needs.

D.why: The notes say haboobs are common in those regions, not that they form only there. The claim about what most people have seen isn't in the notes either.

stem: The student wants to introduce ShakeNet Schools to an audience unfamiliar with the program. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• ShakeNet Schools is a program that places low-cost seismometers in high school classrooms so students can record local earthquakes.
• Seismologist Rafael Okafor launched it in 2012.
• Each classroom sensor costs about $150; a standard research seismometer costs about $12,000.
• By 2024, 310 schools in 14 countries had joined.
• An offshoot, ShakeNet Data Camp, is a summer workshop on analyzing the recordings.
choices: Each ShakeNet Schools sensor costs about $150, nearly $12,000 less than a standard research seismometer.
ShakeNet Schools, launched by seismologist Rafael Okafor, places low-cost seismometers in classrooms to record local earthquakes.
Rafael Okafor's ShakeNet Data Camp is a summer workshop that grew out of the program he launched in 2012.
By 2024, seismologist Rafael Okafor had placed standard research seismometers in 310 high schools across 14 countries.
explanation: Someone who has never heard of ShakeNet Schools needs to know what the program is and what it does. Choice B names it and then states its purpose: it puts low-cost seismometers in classrooms to record local earthquakes. That's the identifying description the goal calls for.

A.why: You focused on the cost gap between the two kinds of instrument. The comparison is accurate, but the choice never explains what the program does, so the reader still doesn't know what ShakeNet Schools is.

C.why: You landed on the offshoot workshop. The choice mentions the program only as something the reader already knows about and never says what it is.

D.why: The notes say the program uses low-cost sensors in place of standard research seismometers. This choice says the opposite, and it also credits Okafor personally with the installations.

verification.problem: Choice D misrepresents the type of seismometer deployed—the notes clearly distinguish ShakeNet's low-cost $150 sensors from standard research seismometers costing $12,000, but D incorrectly states that standard research seismometers were placed in 310 schools.
